[ABSTRACT] We have studied the compound nucleus probability, the survival probability, and the evaporation residue cross sections for 6645 projectile-target combinations to synthesize the superheavy nuclei with atomic numbers $Z=110$--126 in the light of the entrance channel effects such as mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin asymmetry, non-compound nuclear fission probability, and Businaro-Gallone mass asymmetry. The role of quasifission in every reaction has also been considered. Decay chains of various superheavy nuclei produced from the reactions are portrayed as well. The most striking results are that the measured evaporation residue cross sections are of the order of picobarns, whereas the proposed reactions can yield up to microbarn cross sections for the superheavy nuclei with $110\ensuremath{\le}Z\ensuremath{\le}126$. We suggest future experiments may utilize these hot fusion reactions to synthesize new elements ($Z>118$) or to study the properties of the known superheavy nuclei in greater detail. In particular, a proposed reaction containing both projectiles and targets that are naturally abundant, for example, $_{36}^{82}\mathrm{Kr}+_{90}^{232}\mathrm{Th}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}^{314}126+0n$, yields evaporation residue cross sections as high as 31 nb. The presently available experimental setup can test the prediction with ease to make a dream come true by putting a footstep into the eighth row of the periodic table.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. - The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. - The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. - The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. - Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. - The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. [ABSTRACT] We have studied the compound nucleus probability, the survival probability, and the evaporation residue cross sections for 6645 projectile-target combinations to synthesize the superheavy nuclei with atomic numbers $Z=110$--126 in the light of the entrance channel effects such as mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin asymmetry, non-compound nuclear fission probability, and Businaro-Gallone mass asymmetry. The role of quasifission in every reaction has also been considered. Decay chains of various superheavy nuclei produced from the reactions are portrayed as well. The most striking results are that the measured evaporation residue cross sections are of the order of picobarns, whereas the proposed reactions can yield up to microbarn cross sections for the superheavy nuclei with $110\ensuremath{\le}Z\ensuremath{\le}126$. We suggest future experiments may utilize these hot fusion reactions to synthesize new elements ($Z>118$) or to study the properties of the known superheavy nuclei in greater detail. In particular, a proposed reaction containing both projectiles and targets that are naturally abundant, for example, $_{36}^{82}\mathrm{Kr}+_{90}^{232}\mathrm{Th}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}^{314}126+0n$, yields evaporation residue cross sections as high as 31 nb. - Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0 is the 2020 study of entrance-channel-dependent hot fusion reactions for superheavy-element synthesis. It treats the search for elements beyond Z = 118 as a reaction-optimization problem: by surveying thousands of projectile–target combinations, it evaluates compound-nucleus formation probability, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission effects, and entrance-channel asymmetries for Z = 110–126. Its central claim is that carefully chosen hot-fusion routes could produce superheavy nuclei with higher cross sections than many previously measured cases, potentially opening access to the eighth row of the periodic table. Paper 1, the 2025 “Superheavy Nuclei XVII: 1640 ≤ A < 1650 Systems” work, moves the question from “which reactions might synthesize new nuclei?” to “which nuclear interactions and models can credibly describe such extreme systems?” It emphasizes that predictions in the superheavy mass region depend on extrapolating nuclear interactions from better-known nuclei. The transition is therefore from practical synthesis feasibility to theoretical reliability: Paper 0 identifies candidate pathways to new elements, while Paper 1 asks whether the underlying nuclear-structure framework is sufficiently robust to predict stability, decay behavior, and interpretability for those candidates.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. It addresses a major bottleneck for elements beyond Fl/Z = 114: superheavy atoms are produced as rare energetic recoils, often with very short half-lives and low yields, and must be thermalized, transported, and chemically characterized rapidly. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. This transition shows the field moving from “can we make and predict the nucleus?” to “can we capture, transport, and chemically identify it before it decays?” The two 2025 papers are best viewed as parallel developments: one strengthens the theoretical description of superheavy stability, while the other improves the experimental apparatus needed to verify and chemically place new elements.

Key Turning Points:  
- The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. It frames the central question of whether the periodic table is limited by nuclear physics, experimental capability, or discovery standards.  
- The 2020 hot-fusion study marks a methodological turning point: the search for Z > 118 becomes systematically predictive. Instead of relying mainly on past reaction choices, it surveys entrance-channel effects and proposes specific reactions that could yield measurable cross sections, including routes toward very heavy Z = 126 systems.  
- The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. The field must confront the model dependence of nuclear interactions, mass predictions, fission barriers, and stability estimates in a region where empirical anchors are sparse.  
- The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. For the heaviest elements, discovery may require not only nuclear synthesis but also rapid atom-by-atom chemical handling and element-specific characterization.

Recurring Limitations:  
- Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.  
- Quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain unresolved obstacles. Mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin effects, and non-compound fission can suppress the formation of a fully equilibrated compound nucleus.  
- Theoretical extrapolation is a recurring weakness. Nuclear interactions and stability models must be extended into regions with limited experimental data, creating uncertainty in predicted lifetimes, decay modes, fission barriers, and island-of-stability locations.  
- Short half-lives and low event rates limit chemical and physical characterization. Beyond Fl, atoms may decay before conventional chemical separation or spectroscopy can be completed.  
- Discovery criteria become harder to satisfy when only a few atoms are produced. Unambiguous assignment of atomic number requires correlated decay evidence, chemical behavior, or atomic spectroscopy, but each becomes more difficult as yields fall and lifetimes shorten.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- A unified predictive framework for superheavy-element formation is still lacking. The field needs a model that simultaneously treats entrance-channel dynamics, quasifission, compound-nucleus formation, shell stabilization, fission competition, survival probability, and decay-chain observables with quantified uncertainties.  
- Nuclear interactions in the superheavy region remain insufficiently constrained by experiment. A key open problem is identifying measurable observables—masses, spectroscopy, radii, fission properties, or chemical signatures—that can calibrate models near the limits of the periodic table.  
- There is no fully demonstrated pathway from high-yield synthesis to rapid single-atom chemical identification for Z > 118. Future discovery may require coupling optimized fusion reactions, gas stopping, fast chemical separation, and element-specific detection such as decay correlation, X-ray emission, or atomic spectroscopy in one integrated system.  
- Current synthesis strategies may favor nuclei that are too short-lived for chemical verification. A major unresolved problem is how to produce longer-lived isotopes closer to the island of stability, where chemical properties can be measured and periodic-table placement can be confirmed.  
- The field has not settled what “completion” of the periodic table would mean scientifically. The limit could be set by nuclear instability, by vanishing production cross sections, by the inability to chemically identify single atoms, or by the failure of periodic chemical trends in relativistic superheavy systems. These boundaries are not yet distinguished in a predictive way.  
- Discovery standards for future elements remain scientifically challenging. When only a few atoms exist, the field needs robust statistical and epistemic criteria for assigning atomic number, especially when evidence is indirect and may involve competing interpretations of decay chains or chemical behavior.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0 is the 2020 study of entrance-channel-dependent hot fusion reactions for superheavy-element synthesis. It treats the search for elements beyond Z = 118 as a reaction-optimization problem: by surveying thousands of projectile–target combinations, it evaluates compound-nucleus formation probability, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission effects, and entrance-channel asymmetries for Z = 110–126. Its central claim is that carefully chosen hot-fusion routes could produce superheavy nuclei with higher cross sections than many previously measured cases, potentially opening access to the eighth row of the periodic table. Paper 1, the 2025 “Superheavy Nuclei XVII: 1640 ≤ A < 1650 Systems” work, moves the question from “which reactions might synthesize new nuclei?” to “which nuclear interactions and models can credibly describe such extreme systems?” It emphasizes that predictions in the superheavy mass region depend on extrapolating nuclear interactions from better-known nuclei. The transition is therefore from practical synthesis feasibility to theoretical reliability: Paper 0 identifies candidate pathways to new elements, while Paper 1 asks whether the underlying nuclear-structure framework is sufficiently robust to predict stability, decay behavior, and interpretability for those candidates.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. It addresses a major bottleneck for elements beyond Fl/Z = 114: superheavy atoms are produced as rare energetic recoils, often with very short half-lives and low yields, and must be thermalized, transported, and chemically characterized rapidly. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. This transition shows the field moving from “can we make and predict the nucleus?” to “can we capture, transport, and chemically identify it before it decays?” The two 2025 papers are best viewed as parallel developments: one strengthens the theoretical description of superheavy stability, while the other improves the experimental apparatus needed to verify and chemically place new elements.

Key Turning Points:  
- The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. It frames the central question of whether the periodic table is limited by nuclear physics, experimental capability, or discovery standards.  
- The 2020 hot-fusion study marks a methodological turning point: the search for Z > 118 becomes systematically predictive. Instead of relying mainly on past reaction choices, it surveys entrance-channel effects and proposes specific reactions that could yield measurable cross sections, including routes toward very heavy Z = 126 systems.  
- The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. The field must confront the model dependence of nuclear interactions, mass predictions, fission barriers, and stability estimates in a region where empirical anchors are sparse.  
- The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. For the heaviest elements, discovery may require not only nuclear synthesis but also rapid atom-by-atom chemical handling and element-specific characterization.

Recurring Limitations:  
- Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.  
- Quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain unresolved obstacles. Mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin effects, and non-compound fission can suppress the formation of a fully equilibrated compound nucleus.  
- Theoretical extrapolation is a recurring weakness. Nuclear interactions and stability models must be extended into regions with limited experimental data, creating uncertainty in predicted lifetimes, decay modes, fission barriers, and island-of-stability locations.  
- Short half-lives and low event rates limit chemical and physical characterization. Beyond Fl, atoms may decay before conventional chemical separation or spectroscopy can be completed.  
- Discovery criteria become harder to satisfy when only a few atoms are produced. Unambiguous assignment of atomic number requires correlated decay evidence, chemical behavior, or atomic spectroscopy, but each becomes more difficult as yields fall and lifetimes shorten.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- A unified predictive framework for superheavy-element formation is still lacking. The field needs a model that simultaneously treats entrance-channel dynamics, quasifission, compound-nucleus formation, shell stabilization, fission competition, survival probability, and decay-chain observables with quantified uncertainties.  
- Nuclear interactions in the superheavy region remain insufficiently constrained by experiment. A key open problem is identifying measurable observables—masses, spectroscopy, radii, fission properties, or chemical signatures—that can calibrate models near the limits of the periodic table.  
- There is no fully demonstrated pathway from high-yield synthesis to rapid single-atom chemical identification for Z > 118. Future discovery may require coupling optimized fusion reactions, gas stopping, fast chemical separation, and element-specific detection such as decay correlation, X-ray emission, or atomic spectroscopy in one integrated system.  
- Current synthesis strategies may favor nuclei that are too short-lived for chemical verification. A major unresolved problem is how to produce longer-lived isotopes closer to the island of stability, where chemical properties can be measured and periodic-table placement can be confirmed.  
- The field has not settled what “completion” of the periodic table would mean scientifically. The limit could be set by nuclear instability, by vanishing production cross sections, by the inability to chemically identify single atoms, or by the failure of periodic chemical trends in relativistic superheavy systems. These boundaries are not yet distinguished in a predictive way.  
- Discovery standards for future elements remain scientifically challenging. When only a few atoms exist, the field needs robust statistical and epistemic criteria for assigning atomic number, especially when evidence is indirect and may involve competing interpretations of decay chains or chemical behavior.

ideas.title: Verification-Aware Extreme-Event Bayesian Assay for the Completion Limit of the Periodic Table
ideas.motivation: The question of whether the periodic table will ever be complete now hinges on discovery verification as much as on nuclear synthesis, because IUPAC/IUPAP recognition requires sufficient evidence that a new atomic number has been produced and identified [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628). Hot-fusion surveys can propose projectile-target combinations for Z > 118, but predicted evaporation-residue cross sections are extremely small and strongly affected by quasifission, entrance-channel asymmetry, and survival probability [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399). Theoretical predictions must also extrapolate nuclear interactions into poorly constrained superheavy regions, creating uncertainty in masses, fission barriers, and lifetimes [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127). For the heaviest atoms, verification becomes a time-critical single-atom transport and chemistry problem, because recoils must be thermalized and delivered to detection before decay [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). The primary testable hypothesis is that, when the candidate pool, surrogate models, and beam budget are held fixed, an acquisition policy that maximizes the end-to-end probability of an IUPAC-verifiable atom yields more verified atoms than a policy that maximizes production cross section alone. To test this, the idea transfers multi-fidelity Bayesian experimental design for extreme-event statistics from computational uncertainty quantification into superheavy-element discovery [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4213165830).
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the lack of a controlled, experimentally anchored way to decide whether elements beyond Z = 118 can be synthesized and verified before they decay; it can be divided into 4 parts: a fixed synthesis-and-stability candidate layer, a single-atom verification layer, an extreme-event multi-fidelity Bayesian acquisition layer, and a completion-boundary decision layer.

proposed_method.name: Fixed synthesis-and-stability candidate layer
proposed_method.description: Create a non-adapting candidate pool of projectile-target-energy combinations for Z = 119 to 126 using entrance-channel-dependent hot-fusion calculations that estimate compound-nucleus formation, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission, and entrance-channel asymmetries [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399). Attach uncertainty distributions to masses, fission barriers, half-lives, and decay chains by using superheavy-nucleus interaction models for the relevant mass region [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127).

proposed_method.name: Single-atom verification layer
proposed_method.description: Convert each candidate into a probability of obtaining discovery-grade evidence by modeling recoil thermalization, gas-flow transport, ion transfer, and time losses with atmospheric-pressure ion-transfer simulations for a UniCell buffer-gas system [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). Represent IUPAC/IUPAP atomic-number assignment as a probabilistic observation model that rewards correlated decay chains, chemical placement, or other element-specific evidence under low-count conditions [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628).

proposed_method.name: Extreme-event multi-fidelity Bayesian acquisition layer
proposed_method.description: Borrow multi-fidelity Bayesian experimental design for extreme-event statistics from computational uncertainty quantification and use it to select the next reaction or beam energy [Author et al., 2022](https://openalex.org/W4213165830). Treat cheap reaction, stability, and transport simulations as low-fidelity information and beam-time observations as high-fidelity information; the acquisition function maximizes the posterior probability of at least one verified atom, or the expected number of verified atoms, within a fixed beam-time budget.

proposed_method.name: Completion-boundary decision layer
proposed_method.description: Use the posterior verified-event rate to classify each candidate element as physically inaccessible, verification-limited, or discoverable under a given facility. If the predicted verified-event rate remains below a discovery threshold even when verification efficiency is set to unity, the boundary is assigned to nuclear stability or production; if verification losses dominate, the boundary is assigned to capture, transport, or evidence collection, thereby giving an empirical way to address periodic-table completion [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628).

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Experimental Design to Quantify Extreme-Event Statistics
analogy_mapping.concept: Multi-fidelity Bayesian experimental design and acquisition for estimating extremely rare event probabilities
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Adapted to superheavy-element discovery by treating reaction synthesis, nuclear stability, gas transport, and single-atom verification as heterogeneous fidelity sources and selecting experiments that maximize the tail probability of at least one IUPAC-verifiable atom.

experiment_plan: Phase 1 setup: fix the candidate pool of Z = 119 and Z = 120 projectile-target-energy combinations, nuclear-stability priors, gas-cell geometry, transport times, detector efficiencies, decay data, and total beam-time budget so that only the selection policy can vary.

Build a blind benchmark: calibrate surrogate models on historical or simulated outcomes from known superheavy isotopes, withhold a truth set of reaction-energy outcomes, and prevent every policy from seeing the truth set during selection.

Run the full verification-aware extreme-event Bayesian policy and controls: production-only, transport-only, detection-only, fixed-weight unstructured mixture of normalized component scores, and random selection, with identical training data, candidate pool, compute budget, and number of proposed experiments.

Primary one-factor test: vary only the acquisition objective/selection policy and keep all models, priors, and resources fixed; evaluate repeated trials on the blind truth set using expected verified atoms, posterior probability of at least one verified atom, and false-positive discovery rate.

Exclude algorithmic confounders: verify surrogate calibration, repeat with equal numbers of low-fidelity evaluations, use leave-known-success-out splits, fix decay constants and chemical efficiencies, test prior sensitivity, and compare structured Bayesian acquisition with random selection and fixed-weight mixture to rule out chance and simple averaging.

Attribute the effect to the claimed mechanism: ablate production, transport, and detection components alone; the full policy must outperform each single-component policy and the unstructured mixture, and improvement must appear when verification probability is included in the acquisition utility.

Phase 2 physical validation: using a known short-lived recoil or homolog, compare method-selected conditions with production-only and random controls in randomized blocks while holding apparatus, gas cell, separator, detectors, beam dose, and target batch fixed; monitor target degradation, gas-flow drift, detector dead time, and background to exclude trivial explanations.

Phase 3 secondary optimization: after the primary hypothesis is confirmed, allow target thickness, gas pressure, transfer geometry, detector gating, and alternative projectiles to vary, and optimize them with the same verified-event acquisition function.

Phase 4 completion-boundary application: apply the validated model to Z = 119 to 126 candidates, compute posterior probabilities of verifiable atoms under current and near-future facilities, and classify each candidate as physically inaccessible, verification-limited, or discoverable.

prompt:
You are a cross-domain synergy analyst. You need to identify if a candidate paper can inspire the current problem.

Original Problem:
Existing methods do not provide an integrated, experimentally anchored way to determine whether future elements can be synthesized, survive long enough, be captured and chemically identified as single atoms, and satisfy discovery criteria. Hot-fusion reaction studies can propose candidate pathways, but quasifission, tiny cross sections, and survival uncertainties remain. Superheavy-nucleus theory must extrapolate nuclear interactions into poorly constrained regions, while chemical-transport simulations show that identification becomes a time-critical single-atom problem. The field therefore lacks a unified predictive and verifiable framework linking reaction choice, nuclear stability, decay observables, rapid chemical handling, and atomic-number assignment for elements beyond Z = 118.

Candidate Paper:
- Title: Colliding heavy nuclei take multiple identities on the path to fusion
- Abstract: The properties of superheavy elements probe extremes of physics and chemistry. They are synthesised at accelerator laboratories using nuclear fusion, where two atomic nuclei collide, stick together (capture), then with low probability evolve to a compact superheavy nucleus. The fundamental microscopic mechanisms controlling fusion are not fully understood, limiting predictive capability. Even capture, considered to be the simplest stage of fusion, is not matched by models. Here we show that collisions of <sup>40</sup>Ca with <sup>208</sup>Pb, experience an 'explosion' of mass and charge transfers between the nuclei before capture, with unexpectedly high probability and complexity. Ninety different partitions of the protons and neutrons between the projectile-like and target-like nuclei are observed. Since each is expected to have a different probability of fusion, the early stages of collisions may be crucial in superheavy element synthesis. Our interpretation challenges the current view of fusion, explains both the successes and failures of current capture models, and provides a framework for improved models.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0 is the 2020 study of entrance-channel-dependent hot fusion reactions for superheavy-element synthesis. It treats the search for elements beyond Z = 118 as a reaction-optimization problem: by surveying thousands of projectile–target combinations, it evaluates compound-nucleus formation probability, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission effects, and entrance-channel asymmetries for Z = 110–126. Its central claim is that carefully chosen hot-fusion routes could produce superheavy nuclei with higher cross sections than many previously measured cases, potentially opening access to the eighth row of the periodic table. Paper 1, the 2025 “Superheavy Nuclei XVII: 1640 ≤ A < 1650 Systems” work, moves the question from “which reactions might synthesize new nuclei?” to “which nuclear interactions and models can credibly describe such extreme systems?” It emphasizes that predictions in the superheavy mass region depend on extrapolating nuclear interactions from better-known nuclei. The transition is therefore from practical synthesis feasibility to theoretical reliability: Paper 0 identifies candidate pathways to new elements, while Paper 1 asks whether the underlying nuclear-structure framework is sufficiently robust to predict stability, decay behavior, and interpretability for those candidates.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. It addresses a major bottleneck for elements beyond Fl/Z = 114: superheavy atoms are produced as rare energetic recoils, often with very short half-lives and low yields, and must be thermalized, transported, and chemically characterized rapidly. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. This transition shows the field moving from “can we make and predict the nucleus?” to “can we capture, transport, and chemically identify it before it decays?” The two 2025 papers are best viewed as parallel developments: one strengthens the theoretical description of superheavy stability, while the other improves the experimental apparatus needed to verify and chemically place new elements.

Key Turning Points:  
- The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. It frames the central question of whether the periodic table is limited by nuclear physics, experimental capability, or discovery standards.  
- The 2020 hot-fusion study marks a methodological turning point: the search for Z > 118 becomes systematically predictive. Instead of relying mainly on past reaction choices, it surveys entrance-channel effects and proposes specific reactions that could yield measurable cross sections, including routes toward very heavy Z = 126 systems.  
- The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. The field must confront the model dependence of nuclear interactions, mass predictions, fission barriers, and stability estimates in a region where empirical anchors are sparse.  
- The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. For the heaviest elements, discovery may require not only nuclear synthesis but also rapid atom-by-atom chemical handling and element-specific characterization.

Recurring Limitations:  
- Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.  
- Quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain unresolved obstacles. Mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin effects, and non-compound fission can suppress the formation of a fully equilibrated compound nucleus.  
- Theoretical extrapolation is a recurring weakness. Nuclear interactions and stability models must be extended into regions with limited experimental data, creating uncertainty in predicted lifetimes, decay modes, fission barriers, and island-of-stability locations.  
- Short half-lives and low event rates limit chemical and physical characterization. Beyond Fl, atoms may decay before conventional chemical separation or spectroscopy can be completed.  
- Discovery criteria become harder to satisfy when only a few atoms are produced. Unambiguous assignment of atomic number requires correlated decay evidence, chemical behavior, or atomic spectroscopy, but each becomes more difficult as yields fall and lifetimes shorten.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- A unified predictive framework for superheavy-element formation is still lacking. The field needs a model that simultaneously treats entrance-channel dynamics, quasifission, compound-nucleus formation, shell stabilization, fission competition, survival probability, and decay-chain observables with quantified uncertainties.  
- Nuclear interactions in the superheavy region remain insufficiently constrained by experiment. A key open problem is identifying measurable observables—masses, spectroscopy, radii, fission properties, or chemical signatures—that can calibrate models near the limits of the periodic table.  
- There is no fully demonstrated pathway from high-yield synthesis to rapid single-atom chemical identification for Z > 118. Future discovery may require coupling optimized fusion reactions, gas stopping, fast chemical separation, and element-specific detection such as decay correlation, X-ray emission, or atomic spectroscopy in one integrated system.  
- Current synthesis strategies may favor nuclei that are too short-lived for chemical verification. A major unresolved problem is how to produce longer-lived isotopes closer to the island of stability, where chemical properties can be measured and periodic-table placement can be confirmed.  
- The field has not settled what “completion” of the periodic table would mean scientifically. The limit could be set by nuclear instability, by vanishing production cross sections, by the inability to chemically identify single atoms, or by the failure of periodic chemical trends in relativistic superheavy systems. These boundaries are not yet distinguished in a predictive way.  
- Discovery standards for future elements remain scientifically challenging. When only a few atoms exist, the field needs robust statistical and epistemic criteria for assigning atomic number, especially when evidence is indirect and may involve competing interpretations of decay chains or chemical behavior.

[ABSTRACT] We have studied the compound nucleus probability, the survival probability, and the evaporation residue cross sections for 6645 projectile-target combinations to synthesize the superheavy nuclei with atomic numbers $Z=110$--126 in the light of the entrance channel effects such as mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin asymmetry, non-compound nuclear fission probability, and Businaro-Gallone mass asymmetry. The role of quasifission in every reaction has also been considered. Decay chains of various superheavy nuclei produced from the reactions are portrayed as well. The most striking results are that the measured evaporation residue cross sections are of the order of picobarns, whereas the proposed reactions can yield up to microbarn cross sections for the superheavy nuclei with $110\ensuremath{\le}Z\ensuremath{\le}126$. We suggest future experiments may utilize these hot fusion reactions to synthesize new elements ($Z>118$) or to study the properties of the known superheavy nuclei in greater detail. In particular, a proposed reaction containing both projectiles and targets that are naturally abundant, for example, $_{36}^{82}\mathrm{Kr}+_{90}^{232}\mathrm{Th}\ensuremath{\rightarrow}^{314}126+0n$, yields evaporation residue cross sections as high as 31 nb. The presently available experimental setup can test the prediction with ease to make a dream come true by putting a footstep into the eighth row of the periodic table.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0 is the 2020 study of entrance-channel-dependent hot fusion reactions for superheavy-element synthesis. It treats the search for elements beyond Z = 118 as a reaction-optimization problem: by surveying thousands of projectile–target combinations, it evaluates compound-nucleus formation probability, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission effects, and entrance-channel asymmetries for Z = 110–126. Its central claim is that carefully chosen hot-fusion routes could produce superheavy nuclei with higher cross sections than many previously measured cases, potentially opening access to the eighth row of the periodic table. Paper 1, the 2025 “Superheavy Nuclei XVII: 1640 ≤ A < 1650 Systems” work, moves the question from “which reactions might synthesize new nuclei?” to “which nuclear interactions and models can credibly describe such extreme systems?” It emphasizes that predictions in the superheavy mass region depend on extrapolating nuclear interactions from better-known nuclei. The transition is therefore from practical synthesis feasibility to theoretical reliability: Paper 0 identifies candidate pathways to new elements, while Paper 1 asks whether the underlying nuclear-structure framework is sufficiently robust to predict stability, decay behavior, and interpretability for those candidates.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. It addresses a major bottleneck for elements beyond Fl/Z = 114: superheavy atoms are produced as rare energetic recoils, often with very short half-lives and low yields, and must be thermalized, transported, and chemically characterized rapidly. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. This transition shows the field moving from “can we make and predict the nucleus?” to “can we capture, transport, and chemically identify it before it decays?” The two 2025 papers are best viewed as parallel developments: one strengthens the theoretical description of superheavy stability, while the other improves the experimental apparatus needed to verify and chemically place new elements.

Key Turning Points:  
- The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. It frames the central question of whether the periodic table is limited by nuclear physics, experimental capability, or discovery standards.  
- The 2020 hot-fusion study marks a methodological turning point: the search for Z > 118 becomes systematically predictive. Instead of relying mainly on past reaction choices, it surveys entrance-channel effects and proposes specific reactions that could yield measurable cross sections, including routes toward very heavy Z = 126 systems.  
- The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. The field must confront the model dependence of nuclear interactions, mass predictions, fission barriers, and stability estimates in a region where empirical anchors are sparse.  
- The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. For the heaviest elements, discovery may require not only nuclear synthesis but also rapid atom-by-atom chemical handling and element-specific characterization.

Recurring Limitations:  
- Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.  
- Quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain unresolved obstacles. Mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin effects, and non-compound fission can suppress the formation of a fully equilibrated compound nucleus.  
- Theoretical extrapolation is a recurring weakness. Nuclear interactions and stability models must be extended into regions with limited experimental data, creating uncertainty in predicted lifetimes, decay modes, fission barriers, and island-of-stability locations.  
- Short half-lives and low event rates limit chemical and physical characterization. Beyond Fl, atoms may decay before conventional chemical separation or spectroscopy can be completed.  
- Discovery criteria become harder to satisfy when only a few atoms are produced. Unambiguous assignment of atomic number requires correlated decay evidence, chemical behavior, or atomic spectroscopy, but each becomes more difficult as yields fall and lifetimes shorten.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- A unified predictive framework for superheavy-element formation is still lacking. The field needs a model that simultaneously treats entrance-channel dynamics, quasifission, compound-nucleus formation, shell stabilization, fission competition, survival probability, and decay-chain observables with quantified uncertainties.  
- Nuclear interactions in the superheavy region remain insufficiently constrained by experiment. A key open problem is identifying measurable observables—masses, spectroscopy, radii, fission properties, or chemical signatures—that can calibrate models near the limits of the periodic table.  
- There is no fully demonstrated pathway from high-yield synthesis to rapid single-atom chemical identification for Z > 118. Future discovery may require coupling optimized fusion reactions, gas stopping, fast chemical separation, and element-specific detection such as decay correlation, X-ray emission, or atomic spectroscopy in one integrated system.  
- Current synthesis strategies may favor nuclei that are too short-lived for chemical verification. A major unresolved problem is how to produce longer-lived isotopes closer to the island of stability, where chemical properties can be measured and periodic-table placement can be confirmed.  
- The field has not settled what “completion” of the periodic table would mean scientifically. The limit could be set by nuclear instability, by vanishing production cross sections, by the inability to chemically identify single atoms, or by the failure of periodic chemical trends in relativistic superheavy systems. These boundaries are not yet distinguished in a predictive way.  
- Discovery standards for future elements remain scientifically challenging. When only a few atoms exist, the field needs robust statistical and epistemic criteria for assigning atomic number, especially when evidence is indirect and may involve competing interpretations of decay chains or chemical behavior.

ideas.title: Counterfactual Evidence-Accumulation Assay for the Verifiable Completion Boundary of the Periodic Table
ideas.motivation: The question of whether the periodic table can be completed is no longer only a synthesis question. IUPAC/IUPAP guidance emphasizes that element discovery depends on evolving verification methods and criteria [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628). Hot-fusion calculations identify possible projectile-target routes to Z > 118, but cross sections are tiny and quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain problematic [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399). Predictions of stability and decay in this region depend on extrapolated nuclear interactions with limited experimental anchors [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127), and chemical identification becomes a time-critical single-atom transport problem [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). The unresolved bottleneck is therefore not a missing reaction list but the absence of a verification-aware decision framework that treats a discoverable element as an evidence-accumulation event and separates nuclear-stability limits from verification limits. The proposed method transfers hierarchical Bayesian evidence accumulation from atomic-physics data analysis [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W2558575588) and single-event residence-time analysis from single-molecule separation science [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3087606226) to superheavy-element discovery.
ideas.method_overview: This method is intended to solve the lack of an experimentally anchored way to decide whether elements beyond Z = 118 can be both synthesized and verified, and whether the periodic table's limit is nuclear-stability-limited or verification-limited; it can be divided into 4 parts: a hierarchical probabilistic digital twin, a single-atom evidence model, an information-gain acquisition policy, and a counterfactual completion-boundary decomposition. The primary testable hypothesis is that selecting experiments by expected reduction in atomic-number assignment ambiguity yields a higher probability of reaching an IUPAC-scale verification threshold per fixed beam time than selecting by expected atom counts, when synthesis, transport, and detection models are held fixed.

proposed_method.name: Hierarchical synthesis-verification digital twin
proposed_method.description: Build a probabilistic model with latent variables for projectile-target entrance channel, compound-nucleus formation, quasifission, evaporation-residue cross section, survival, decay, thermalization, gas-flow transport, and detection. Candidate reaction pathways and cross-section estimates for Z = 119-126 are taken from entrance-channel-dependent hot-fusion surveys [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399). Nuclear masses, fission barriers, and half-lives are encoded as uncertain priors reflecting extrapolated superheavy nuclear interactions [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127). Recoil stopping, ion transfer, and gas-flow delays are modeled using buffer-gas-cell simulation studies [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). Target degradation, gas-flow drift, detector dead time, and correlated background are latent nonstationary state variables updated sequentially, using hierarchical Bayesian methods for sparse atomic measurements [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W2558575588).

proposed_method.name: Single-atom evidence model with decay-chain-graph and first-passage chemical likelihoods
proposed_method.description: Represent each observed atom as a directed graph of correlated decay events and chemical residence-time measurements, with atomic number Z as the latent hypothesis to be verified under IUPAC/IUPAP discovery standards [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628). The chemical branch treats thermalization and transport through the gas-flow device as a stochastic first-passage and residence-time process, so that adsorption/desorption delays and single-atom capture times become element-specific likelihood evidence rather than simple efficiency losses [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). This adapts single-molecule separation analysis, where identity is inferred from rare single-event transport and binding fluctuations [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3087606226). Bayesian model comparison assigns probabilities to competing Z and decay-chain interpretations [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W2558575588).

proposed_method.name: Verification-information-gain acquisition policy
proposed_method.description: Define the next-action acquisition function as the expected reduction in entropy of the posterior over Z and isotope, or equivalently expected increase in log Bayes factor for an IUPAC-scale verification threshold, rather than expected produced or detected atoms [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628). The expected gain is computed over possible future decay-chain graphs and first-passage chemical observations. Actions include selecting a projectile-target combination, allocating beam dose, adjusting gas-flow/chemistry conditions, running calibration sources, or measuring background. The policy uses posterior predictive simulations from the digital twin and can choose calibration when drift or dead-time uncertainty makes calibration more informative than additional beam time, extending Bayesian atomic-physics experimental design to sequential single-atom superheavy verification [Author et al., 2017](https://openalex.org/W2558575588).

proposed_method.name: Counterfactual completion-boundary decomposition
proposed_method.description: For each candidate element/isotope, compute discovery probability under actual conditions and under explicit interventions: perfect production, perfect transport, perfect detection, and perfect calibration. Production counterfactuals are bounded by optimistic hot-fusion cross-section predictions [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399); transport/detection counterfactuals idealize the gas-flow and detector stages [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862); stability uncertainty is propagated from superheavy nuclear-interaction models [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127). If perfect verification does not make discovery probable, the candidate is stability/production-limited; if perfect verification does, it is verification-limited. This turns the qualitative question of periodic-table completion into a quantitatively decomposed boundary problem [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628).

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Bayesian data analysis tools for atomic physics
analogy_mapping.concept: Hierarchical Bayesian inference, posterior updating, uncertainty quantification, and model comparison for sparse atomic measurements.
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Used to build a joint posterior over atomic number, isotope, decay-chain graph, transport state, and nonstationary nuisance parameters, and to define an information-gain acquisition function for superheavy-element verification.

analogy_mapping.inspiration: Transforming Separation Science with Single-Molecule Methods
analogy_mapping.concept: Single-event residence-time, adsorption/desorption, and first-passage analysis of rare entities.
analogy_mapping.adaptation: Each superheavy recoil atom is treated as a single stochastic chemical-transport event; residence-time and first-passage distributions become element-specific likelihood evidence for Z assignment.

experiment_plan: Phase 0: Freeze benchmark. Select a fixed set of Z=119-126 projectile-target combinations and cross-section ranges from hot-fusion reaction surveys [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3111464399), assign nuclear-stability priors from superheavy-interaction extrapolations [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127), and fix gas-flow/thermalization delay distributions from UniCell simulation studies [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4412961862). Define an IUPAC-inspired verification threshold, such as posterior probability for a single Z assignment or Bayes factor, and freeze all nonstationary nuisance parameters for the primary test [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628).

Phase 1 primary one-factor test: Vary only the acquisition objective. Compare evidence-information-gain acquisition against expected detected atoms, expected verified atoms without graph/chemical information gain, cross-section-yield-only selection, and random selection. Use identical hidden simulated truths, identical candidate reactions, identical beam-time budget, and identical production/transport/detection models. Primary endpoint: probability of crossing the verification threshold per fixed beam time.

Controls for trivial confounders: equalize computation and candidate set across policies; include an open-loop precomputed schedule to test whether sequential updating itself matters; include a random-tie-break policy to test whether search effort alone explains gains; include an unstructured mixture control, the computational analogue of a physical mixture, that combines independent synthesis, transport, and chemistry scores without a shared posterior; include a randomized evidence-graph control with shuffled decay/chemical links; and report sensitivity to cross-section priors, half-life priors, adsorption/mass-transport parameters, target degradation, gas-flow drift, detector dead time, and correlated background. These controls distinguish the claimed evidence-accumulation mechanism from higher yield, longer lifetime, better transport, or background suppression.

Component-ablation controls: with acquisition fixed, run the model using decay-chain evidence only, first-passage chemical evidence only, both without nonstationary calibration actions, and both with calibration actions. This tests whether gains come from the claimed single-atom evidence model and calibration scheduling rather than from generic Bayesian updating.

Retrospective validation: apply the frozen model to archived known-superheavy-element events and to simulated homologs to test whether posterior Z assignment recovers accepted discoveries and whether the information-gain policy retrospectively prioritizes evidence-rich conditions [Author et al., 2020](https://openalex.org/W3048546628). Use posterior predictive checks and held-out events to rule out overconfidence.

Counterfactual boundary analysis: after the primary hypothesis is supported, compute discovery probabilities under do(perfect production), do(perfect transport), do(perfect detection), and do(perfect calibration). Decompose the gap into stability/production-limited, verification-limited, and mixed categories, with uncertainty intervals from the posterior [Author et al., 2025](https://openalex.org/W4415525127).

Secondary scope: only after Phase 1, vary nuclear-interaction priors, entrance-channel asymmetries, target degradation rates, gas-flow geometries, detector backgrounds, and beam intensities one factor at a time to test robustness of the completion-boundary classification. Do not use these variations in the primary hypothesis test.

Prospective pilot: use the validated policy to propose a calibration-first experimental sequence for one Z=119 candidate reaction at an existing facility. Success is measured by increased expected information gain and a clear boundary classification, not by guaranteed discovery.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0 is the 2020 study of entrance-channel-dependent hot fusion reactions for superheavy-element synthesis. It treats the search for elements beyond Z = 118 as a reaction-optimization problem: by surveying thousands of projectile–target combinations, it evaluates compound-nucleus formation probability, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission effects, and entrance-channel asymmetries for Z = 110–126. Its central claim is that carefully chosen hot-fusion routes could produce superheavy nuclei with higher cross sections than many previously measured cases, potentially opening access to the eighth row of the periodic table. Paper 1, the 2025 “Superheavy Nuclei XVII: 1640 ≤ A < 1650 Systems” work, moves the question from “which reactions might synthesize new nuclei?” to “which nuclear interactions and models can credibly describe such extreme systems?” It emphasizes that predictions in the superheavy mass region depend on extrapolating nuclear interactions from better-known nuclei. The transition is therefore from practical synthesis feasibility to theoretical reliability: Paper 0 identifies candidate pathways to new elements, while Paper 1 asks whether the underlying nuclear-structure framework is sufficiently robust to predict stability, decay behavior, and interpretability for those candidates.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. It addresses a major bottleneck for elements beyond Fl/Z = 114: superheavy atoms are produced as rare energetic recoils, often with very short half-lives and low yields, and must be thermalized, transported, and chemically characterized rapidly. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. This transition shows the field moving from “can we make and predict the nucleus?” to “can we capture, transport, and chemically identify it before it decays?” The two 2025 papers are best viewed as parallel developments: one strengthens the theoretical description of superheavy stability, while the other improves the experimental apparatus needed to verify and chemically place new elements.

Key Turning Points:  
- The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. It frames the central question of whether the periodic table is limited by nuclear physics, experimental capability, or discovery standards.  
- The 2020 hot-fusion study marks a methodological turning point: the search for Z > 118 becomes systematically predictive. Instead of relying mainly on past reaction choices, it surveys entrance-channel effects and proposes specific reactions that could yield measurable cross sections, including routes toward very heavy Z = 126 systems.  
- The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. The field must confront the model dependence of nuclear interactions, mass predictions, fission barriers, and stability estimates in a region where empirical anchors are sparse.  
- The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. For the heaviest elements, discovery may require not only nuclear synthesis but also rapid atom-by-atom chemical handling and element-specific characterization.

Recurring Limitations:  
- Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.  
- Quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain unresolved obstacles. Mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin effects, and non-compound fission can suppress the formation of a fully equilibrated compound nucleus.  
- Theoretical extrapolation is a recurring weakness. Nuclear interactions and stability models must be extended into regions with limited experimental data, creating uncertainty in predicted lifetimes, decay modes, fission barriers, and island-of-stability locations.  
- Short half-lives and low event rates limit chemical and physical characterization. Beyond Fl, atoms may decay before conventional chemical separation or spectroscopy can be completed.  
- Discovery criteria become harder to satisfy when only a few atoms are produced. Unambiguous assignment of atomic number requires correlated decay evidence, chemical behavior, or atomic spectroscopy, but each becomes more difficult as yields fall and lifetimes shorten.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- A unified predictive framework for superheavy-element formation is still lacking. The field needs a model that simultaneously treats entrance-channel dynamics, quasifission, compound-nucleus formation, shell stabilization, fission competition, survival probability, and decay-chain observables with quantified uncertainties.  
- Nuclear interactions in the superheavy region remain insufficiently constrained by experiment. A key open problem is identifying measurable observables—masses, spectroscopy, radii, fission properties, or chemical signatures—that can calibrate models near the limits of the periodic table.  
- There is no fully demonstrated pathway from high-yield synthesis to rapid single-atom chemical identification for Z > 118. Future discovery may require coupling optimized fusion reactions, gas stopping, fast chemical separation, and element-specific detection such as decay correlation, X-ray emission, or atomic spectroscopy in one integrated system.  
- Current synthesis strategies may favor nuclei that are too short-lived for chemical verification. A major unresolved problem is how to produce longer-lived isotopes closer to the island of stability, where chemical properties can be measured and periodic-table placement can be confirmed.  
- The field has not settled what “completion” of the periodic table would mean scientifically. The limit could be set by nuclear instability, by vanishing production cross sections, by the inability to chemically identify single atoms, or by the failure of periodic chemical trends in relativistic superheavy systems. These boundaries are not yet distinguished in a predictive way.  
- Discovery standards for future elements remain scientifically challenging. When only a few atoms exist, the field needs robust statistical and epistemic criteria for assigning atomic number, especially when evidence is indirect and may involve competing interpretations of decay chains or chemical behavior.

- Trend Analysis: Trends:  
Paper 0 to Paper 1: Paper 0 is the 2020 study of entrance-channel-dependent hot fusion reactions for superheavy-element synthesis. It treats the search for elements beyond Z = 118 as a reaction-optimization problem: by surveying thousands of projectile–target combinations, it evaluates compound-nucleus formation probability, survival probability, evaporation-residue cross sections, quasifission effects, and entrance-channel asymmetries for Z = 110–126. Its central claim is that carefully chosen hot-fusion routes could produce superheavy nuclei with higher cross sections than many previously measured cases, potentially opening access to the eighth row of the periodic table. Paper 1, the 2025 “Superheavy Nuclei XVII: 1640 ≤ A < 1650 Systems” work, moves the question from “which reactions might synthesize new nuclei?” to “which nuclear interactions and models can credibly describe such extreme systems?” It emphasizes that predictions in the superheavy mass region depend on extrapolating nuclear interactions from better-known nuclei. The transition is therefore from practical synthesis feasibility to theoretical reliability: Paper 0 identifies candidate pathways to new elements, while Paper 1 asks whether the underlying nuclear-structure framework is sufficiently robust to predict stability, decay behavior, and interpretability for those candidates.

Paper 1 to Paper 2: Paper 2, the 2025 simulation study of atmospheric-pressure ion transfer in a gas-flow device connected to the UniCell buffer gas cell, shifts the emphasis from nuclear production and stability to experimental handling and chemical identification. It addresses a major bottleneck for elements beyond Fl/Z = 114: superheavy atoms are produced as rare energetic recoils, often with very short half-lives and low yields, and must be thermalized, transported, and chemically characterized rapidly. The advance is not another fusion reaction calculation but an infrastructure-level response: modeling gas-flow and ion-transfer conditions that could preserve and deliver single atoms for chemical study. This transition shows the field moving from “can we make and predict the nucleus?” to “can we capture, transport, and chemically identify it before it decays?” The two 2025 papers are best viewed as parallel developments: one strengthens the theoretical description of superheavy stability, while the other improves the experimental apparatus needed to verify and chemically place new elements.

Key Turning Points:  
- The IUPAC/IUPAP seed report establishes the conceptual turning point: element discovery is no longer only a matter of observing decay chains, but increasingly depends on new synthesis methods, detection regimes, and criteria for verification. It frames the central question of whether the periodic table is limited by nuclear physics, experimental capability, or discovery standards.  
- The 2020 hot-fusion study marks a methodological turning point: the search for Z > 118 becomes systematically predictive. Instead of relying mainly on past reaction choices, it surveys entrance-channel effects and proposes specific reactions that could yield measurable cross sections, including routes toward very heavy Z = 126 systems.  
- The 2025 superheavy-nuclei theory work marks a second turning point: it makes explicit that synthesis predictions alone are insufficient. The field must confront the model dependence of nuclear interactions, mass predictions, fission barriers, and stability estimates in a region where empirical anchors are sparse.  
- The 2025 gas-flow/chemistry simulation marks a third turning point: identification of future elements is recognized as a time-critical chemical and instrumental problem. For the heaviest elements, discovery may require not only nuclear synthesis but also rapid atom-by-atom chemical handling and element-specific characterization.

Recurring Limitations:  
- Extremely low production probabilities persist. Even optimistic predicted evaporation-residue cross sections remain small, and measured superheavy synthesis often occurs at picobarn-level or lower yields.  
- Quasifission and entrance-channel effects remain unresolved obstacles. Mass asymmetry, charge asymmetry, isospin effects, and non-compound fission can suppress the formation of a fully equilibrated compound nucleus.  
- Theoretical extrapolation is a recurring weakness. Nuclear interactions and stability models must be extended into regions with limited experimental data, creating uncertainty in predicted lifetimes, decay modes, fission barriers, and island-of-stability locations.  
- Short half-lives and low event rates limit chemical and physical characterization. Beyond Fl, atoms may decay before conventional chemical separation or spectroscopy can be completed.  
- Discovery criteria become harder to satisfy when only a few atoms are produced. Unambiguous assignment of atomic number requires correlated decay evidence, chemical behavior, or atomic spectroscopy, but each becomes more difficult as yields fall and lifetimes shorten.

Structural Gaps (open SCIENTIFIC problems in the field that remain unsolved — NOT missing papers, absent milestones, or graph-wiring issues):  
- A unified predictive framework for superheavy-element formation is still lacking. The field needs a model that simultaneously treats entrance-channel dynamics, quasifission, compound-nucleus formation, shell stabilization, fission competition, survival probability, and decay-chain observables with quantified uncertainties.  
- Nuclear interactions in the superheavy region remain insufficiently constrained by experiment. A key open problem is identifying measurable observables—masses, spectroscopy, radii, fission properties, or chemical signatures—that can calibrate models near the limits of the periodic table.  
- There is no fully demonstrated pathway from high-yield synthesis to rapid single-atom chemical identification for Z > 118. Future discovery may require coupling optimized fusion reactions, gas stopping, fast chemical separation, and element-specific detection such as decay correlation, X-ray emission, or atomic spectroscopy in one integrated system.  
- Current synthesis strategies may favor nuclei that are too short-lived for chemical verification. A major unresolved problem is how to produce longer-lived isotopes closer to the island of stability, where chemical properties can be measured and periodic-table placement can be confirmed.  
- The field has not settled what “completion” of the periodic table would mean scientifically. The limit could be set by nuclear instability, by vanishing production cross sections, by the inability to chemically identify single atoms, or by the failure of periodic chemical trends in relativistic superheavy systems. These boundaries are not yet distinguished in a predictive way.  
- Discovery standards for future elements remain scientifically challenging. When only a few atoms exist, the field needs robust statistical and epistemic criteria for assigning atomic number, especially when evidence is indirect and may involve competing interpretations of decay chains or chemical behavior.
